why_how.text: The handbook says North Carolina law treats bicycles as vehicles, so bicyclists follow the same traffic laws as drivers.
Drivers should expect bicyclists in the roadway and pass them only with plenty of clearance.

scenario.text: Harper comes up behind a bicyclist on a two-lane road, and the other lane is clear of oncoming traffic.

reasoning.text: Pass a bicyclist only with plenty of clearance and no oncoming traffic in the other lane; changing lanes is the safest way to pass.

result.text: Harper changes lanes to pass, following the same passing laws as for any other vehicle.

claim.text: Many people think a bicyclist must always stay at the edge of the road.

correction.text: Traffic conditions may require a bicyclist to use the full travel lane, and bicyclists may ride in a bike lane, on a paved shoulder or in a regular travel lane.

prompt.text: Harper is behind a bicyclist with the other lane clear of oncoming traffic. What is the safest way to pass?

answer.text: Change lanes, with plenty of clearance.

rationale.text: Passing a bicyclist follows the same passing laws as passing any other vehicle.

narration.text: This chapter covers sharing the road with bicyclists, pedestrians, trucks, recreational vehicles, trailers, motorcycles and mopeds, and ends with littering. This first lesson covers bicyclists on the road. You will review how North Carolina law treats bicycles, where drivers should expect bicyclists, where bicyclists may ride and what guides their choice, the duties bicyclists share with drivers, how to pass a bicyclist, which laws govern that pass, why bicyclists ride with the flow of traffic, and the collision types to watch for.

lines.text: Stop for signs and lights; signal.

narration.text: North Carolina law treats bicycles as vehicles, so bicyclists must obey the same traffic laws as drivers, including the DWI laws. Like drivers, bicyclists must ride on the right side of the road, stop for stop signs and red lights, and give hand signals. So a bicyclist on the road has the same duties you do. The rules about signs, lights and signals apply to them as they apply to you, and so do the impaired driving laws. When you think about how a bicyclist should behave, start from the rules you already follow as a driver.

lines.text: Bike lane, shoulder or travel lane.

narration.text: Drivers should expect bicyclists in the roadway, and traffic conditions may require a bicyclist to use the full travel lane. Bicyclists may ride in a bike lane, on a paved shoulder or in a regular travel lane, choosing based on road conditions, hazards and conflicts with right-turning cars. So a bicyclist in the middle of a travel lane is not breaking a rule when conditions require it. The bicyclist chooses among the bike lane, the paved shoulder and the travel lane based on conditions, hazards and conflicts with right-turning cars.

lines.text: A bicyclist may need the full lane.
Bike lane, shoulder or travel lane.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Many people think a bicyclist must always stay at the edge of the road. The handbook says traffic conditions may require a bicyclist to use the full travel lane, and bicyclists may ride in a bike lane, on a paved shoulder or in a regular travel lane. Practice questions may suggest that a bicyclist must ride only on the shoulder, or only in a bike lane. Neither matches the handbook. The choice is based on road conditions, hazards and conflicts with right-turning cars. Expect bicyclists in the roadway and give them room.

lines.text: Same passing laws as any vehicle.

narration.text: Pass a bicyclist only with plenty of clearance and no oncoming traffic in the other lane. Changing lanes is the safest way to pass. Passing a bicyclist lawfully means following the same vehicle passing laws that apply to passing any other vehicle. Bicyclists should ride with the flow of traffic, never facing it, because drivers often fail to look toward a wrong-way rider. Expect bicycles on every road except where they are expressly banned, and watch for left-cross, drive-out and right-hook collisions. So look for bicyclists everywhere, and pass them like any vehicle.

Here is a quick check: Harper comes up behind a bicyclist on a two-lane road. The other lane has no oncoming traffic. What is the safest way for Harper to pass? Work it out before reading on. Harper should change lanes, passing with plenty of clearance. Pass a bicyclist only with plenty of clearance and no oncoming traffic in the other lane, and changing lanes is the safest way to pass. Passing a bicyclist lawfully means following the same vehicle passing laws that apply to passing any other vehicle, because bicycles are vehicles under North Carolina law.

lines.text: Bicycles are vehicles under the same laws.

narration.text: Let us recap. North Carolina law treats bicycles as vehicles, so bicyclists obey the same traffic laws as drivers, including the DWI laws, riding on the right, stopping for stop signs and red lights, and giving hand signals. Expect bicyclists in the roadway; traffic conditions may require them to use the full travel lane, and they may ride in a bike lane, on a paved shoulder or in a travel lane. Pass only with plenty of clearance, and changing lanes is safest. Bicyclists ride with the flow of traffic, and you should expect them on every road unless expressly banned.

why_how.text: The handbook sets night lighting distances for bicycles, with a farther distance for the front light.
Helmet and restraining seat rules protect young riders and small passengers.

scenario.text: A parent plans to carry a small child on a bicycle; the child is under forty pounds.

reasoning.text: A bicycle passenger under forty pounds or under forty inches tall must ride in a bicycle restraining seat.

result.text: The child rides in a restraining seat and, being under sixteen, also wears an approved helmet.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the helmet rule and the restraining seat rule use the same limit.

correction.text: The bicycle helmet rule covers riders and passengers under sixteen, while the restraining seat rule covers passengers under forty pounds or forty inches.

memory_support.text: Helmet by age, seat by size.

prompt.text: A bicycle passenger is eight years old and weighs thirty pounds. Which equipment rules apply?

answer.text: An approved helmet and a restraining seat.

rationale.text: The helmet rule goes by age under sixteen, and the seat rule goes by size under forty pounds or forty inches.

narration.text: This lesson covers bicycle equipment rules. You will review the lights a bicycle must have at night and how far away each must be visible, who must wear an approved bicycle helmet, and which passengers must ride in a bicycle restraining seat. Each of these rules has a number in it, and practice questions often swap the numbers between rules, so the lesson spends time on keeping them apart: the front light distance versus the rear distance, and the helmet age limit versus the restraining seat size limit. Listen for which rule each number belongs to.

lines.text: Front light: at least three hundred feet.
Rear red light or reflector: two hundred feet.

narration.text: At night a bicycle must have a front light visible from at least three hundred feet and a rear red light or reflector visible from at least two hundred feet. So the front and rear have different requirements. The front must be a light, visible from at least three hundred feet. The rear may be a red light or a reflector, visible from at least two hundred feet. Both are required at night. The front distance is the larger of the two, so if a question asks which distance is three hundred feet, it is the front light, and two hundred feet is the rear.

lines.text: Under sixteen: approved helmet, saddle seat.
Under forty pounds or forty inches: restraining seat.

narration.text: Every bicycle rider and passenger under age sixteen must wear an approved bicycle helmet and sit on a saddle seat. A bicycle passenger under forty pounds or under forty inches tall must ride in a bicycle restraining seat. So the helmet rule covers both riders and passengers, and its limit is age: under sixteen. The restraining seat rule covers passengers only, and its limit is size: under forty pounds or under forty inches tall. A small child passenger can fall under both rules at once, needing an approved helmet and a restraining seat.

lines.text: Seat: under forty pounds or forty inches.

narration.text: Here is the trap. The bicycle helmet rule covers riders and passengers under sixteen, while the restraining seat rule covers passengers under forty pounds or forty inches. Practice questions may give the helmet rule a weight limit, or give the seat rule an age limit. Neither matches the handbook. The helmet rule goes by age. The seat rule goes by size, either weight or height. And for lights, a bicycle at night needs a front light seen from three hundred feet but a rear red light or reflector seen from only two hundred feet. Match each number to its rule.

Here is a quick check: a bicycle passenger is eight years old and weighs thirty pounds. Which equipment rules apply to this passenger? Work it out before reading on. Both rules apply: an approved bicycle helmet and a bicycle restraining seat. Every bicycle rider and passenger under age sixteen must wear an approved bicycle helmet, and the passenger is under sixteen. A bicycle passenger under forty pounds or under forty inches tall must ride in a bicycle restraining seat, and the passenger is under forty pounds. The helmet rule goes by age, and the seat rule goes by size.

lines.text: Rear red light or reflector: two hundred feet.
Helmet by age, seat by size.

narration.text: To wrap up, at night a bicycle must have a front light visible from at least three hundred feet and a rear red light or reflector visible from at least two hundred feet. Every bicycle rider and passenger under age sixteen must wear an approved bicycle helmet and sit on a saddle seat. A bicycle passenger under forty pounds or under forty inches tall must ride in a bicycle restraining seat. The memory line for the two safety rules: helmet by age, seat by size. Next, the people most at risk on the road: pedestrians, and where and how they should walk.

why_how.text: The handbook says pedestrians make up a large share of crash deaths, especially in cities.
Pedestrians walk facing traffic and should make themselves visible, especially at night.

scenario.text: Rowan is walking along a road with no sidewalk at dusk.

reasoning.text: Pedestrians should walk on the left side of the road facing traffic and wear or carry something white; at night, carry a flashlight and be ready to step aside.

result.text: Rowan walks on the left facing traffic, carries a flashlight and is ready to step aside.

claim.text: Many people think pedestrians should move in the same direction as bicyclists.

correction.text: Pedestrians walk on the left facing traffic, which is the opposite of the ride-with-traffic rule for bicyclists.

prompt.text: Rowan is walking beside a road with no sidewalk. Which side should Rowan use, and facing which way?

rationale.text: Pedestrians walk facing traffic, the opposite of bicyclists, who ride with it.

narration.text: This lesson covers pedestrians. You will review the share of motor vehicle crash deaths that are pedestrians in cities and in rural areas, who most of the pedestrians killed are, which side of the road pedestrians should walk on and what they should wear or carry, what to do on foot at night, and how the pedestrian walking rule compares with the bicyclist riding rule. Practice questions often test the city and rural shares, and they often try to mix up which way pedestrians and bicyclists should travel. Those two points get the most attention in this lesson.

lines.text: Cities: about two of every five deaths.

narration.text: In cities about two of every five people killed in motor vehicle crashes are pedestrians, compared with about one in ten in rural areas. Most pedestrians killed are children, elderly people or people who had been drinking. So the pedestrian share of crash deaths is much larger in cities than in rural areas. Pedestrians make up about two of every five crash deaths in cities but only about one in ten in rural areas. And three groups make up most of the pedestrians killed: children, elderly people, and people who had been drinking. Watch especially for those groups.

Here is the trap. Pedestrians make up about two of every five crash deaths in cities but only about one in ten in rural areas. Practice questions may swap the two figures, giving cities one in ten and rural areas two in five. That reverses the handbook. The city share is the larger one. If a question asks about pedestrians in cities, the answer is about two of every five people killed in motor vehicle crashes. If it asks about rural areas, the answer is about one in ten. Keep the larger share tied to cities. The city share is the larger of the two figures.

lines.text: Walk on the left, facing traffic.
At night: flashlight, ready to step aside.

narration.text: Pedestrians should walk on the left side of the road facing traffic and wear or carry something white. On foot at night, carry a flashlight and be ready to step aside, since drivers may not see you. So the pedestrian walks on the left, facing traffic, with something white worn or carried. At night the pedestrian adds a flashlight. And because drivers may not see a pedestrian at night, the pedestrian is ready to step aside. These rules apply whenever you walk along a road. Walk on the left, facing traffic, and carry a flashlight at night.

Here is a second trap. Pedestrians walk on the left facing traffic, which is the opposite of the ride-with-traffic rule for bicyclists. Practice questions may tell a bicyclist to ride facing traffic, or tell a pedestrian to walk with it. Both reverse the handbook. Bicyclists should ride with the flow of traffic, never facing it, because drivers often fail to look toward a wrong-way rider. Pedestrians walk on the left facing traffic. The memory line: walk against, ride with. A person on foot faces the traffic; a person on a bicycle moves with it.

Here is a quick check: Rowan is walking along a road that has no sidewalk. Which side of the road should Rowan use, and facing which way? Work it out before reading on. Rowan should walk on the left side of the road, facing traffic, and wear or carry something white. If it is dark, Rowan should carry a flashlight and be ready to step aside, since drivers may not see a pedestrian. This is the opposite of the rule for bicyclists, who ride with the flow of traffic, never facing it. Walk against, ride with. Pedestrians walk on the left facing traffic, unlike bicyclists.

lines.text: Cities: two in five; rural: one in ten.

narration.text: To finish, in cities about two of every five people killed in motor vehicle crashes are pedestrians, compared with about one in ten in rural areas. Most pedestrians killed are children, elderly people or people who had been drinking. Pedestrians should walk on the left side of the road facing traffic and wear or carry something white. On foot at night, carry a flashlight and be ready to step aside. This is the opposite of the bicyclist rule, which is to ride with traffic. Next, sharing the road with heavy trucks, and the no-zones where truck drivers cannot see you.

why_how.text: The handbook says heavy trucks speed up, turn and stop differently from cars.
Truck drivers sit high but cannot see everything, so the no-zones around a truck matter.

scenario.text: Morgan is driving alongside a tractor-trailer and cannot see the truck driver in the truck's side mirror.

reasoning.text: If you cannot see the driver in the side mirror, the driver cannot see you, and lingering in a no-zone makes it harder for the trucker to steer clear of danger.

result.text: Morgan moves out of the no-zone instead of lingering there.

claim.text: Many people think a truck driver sitting up high can see everything around the truck.

correction.text: Truck drivers sit about twice as high as car drivers, but it is a false assumption that they can see everything around them.

prompt.text: Morgan is beside a truck and cannot see its driver in the side mirror. What does that tell Morgan?

answer.text: The truck driver cannot see Morgan.

rationale.text: Lingering in a no-zone makes it harder for the trucker to steer clear of danger.

narration.text: This lesson covers sharing the road with heavy trucks. You will review how trucks gain speed, why their size can mislead you, why they need extra room to turn and what to check before passing a truck that seems to turn left, what happens to truck brakes on downhill runs, how wind from a large truck affects you, the false assumption about how much truck drivers can see, where the no-zones around a tractor-trailer reach, and why you should not linger in them. Practice questions often test the no-zone distances, so the front and rear lengths get their own slide.

lines.text: Trucks gain speed slowly, especially uphill.
Size can make them seem slower.

narration.text: Heavy trucks gain speed slowly, especially uphill, and their size can make them seem slower than they really are. So a truck ahead of you may be moving faster than it looks, and on an uphill grade, it may be gaining speed only slowly. Do not judge a truck's speed by its size alone, because its size can make it seem slower than it really is. And expect a truck climbing a hill to speed up slowly, especially uphill, compared with a car. Heavy trucks gain speed slowly, especially uphill, and their size can make them seem slower than they really are. Keep both points in mind around trucks.

lines.text: Rear wheels do not follow the front.
Check the signal before passing a turning truck.
Hot brakes downhill; wind affects steering.

narration.text: A truck's rear wheels do not follow its front wheels, so it needs extra room to turn. Check its turn signal before passing a truck that seems to start a left turn. Truck brakes heat up on downhill runs, which means the truck needs more distance to stop. Wind currents from a large truck beside you can affect your steering, so give trucks plenty of room. So trucks need more room in three ways: to turn, because the rear wheels do not follow the front; to stop, especially downhill; and beside you, because their wind can affect your steering.

lines.text: About twice as high as car drivers.

narration.text: Truck drivers sit about twice as high as car drivers, but it is a false assumption that they can see everything around them. So the high seat does not mean the driver can see every car around the truck. There are areas the truck driver cannot see, and the handbook calls them no-zones. The next slide shows where they reach. For now, the point is that a high driver's seat is not the same as seeing everything. Do not assume a truck driver can see you just because the driver sits high. Truck drivers sit about twice as high as car drivers, yet they cannot see everything around them.

lines.text: Both sides, especially beside the cab.
Rear: up to two hundred feet.

narration.text: A tractor-trailer's no-zones reach up to twenty feet in front of the cab, along both sides especially beside the cab, and up to two hundred feet behind. Lingering in a truck's no-zone makes it harder for the trucker to steer clear of danger. If you cannot see the driver in the side mirror, the driver cannot see you. So there are no-zones in front, along both sides and behind. The side mirror gives you a quick test: if you cannot see the driver in it, you are in a place where the driver cannot see you, and you should not linger there.

lines.text: Front no-zone: up to twenty feet.
Rear no-zone: up to two hundred feet.

narration.text: Here is the trap. A truck's front no-zone extends up to twenty feet, but its rear no-zone extends up to two hundred feet. Practice questions may swap the two distances, giving the front two hundred feet and the rear twenty feet. That reverses the handbook. The rear no-zone is the longer one, reaching up to two hundred feet behind the truck. The front no-zone reaches up to twenty feet in front of the cab. And along both sides, the no-zone is especially beside the cab. The memory line for this slide: the rear zone is longer.

Here is a quick check: Morgan is driving alongside a tractor-trailer and looks at the truck's side mirror but cannot see the truck driver in it. What does that tell Morgan? Work it out before reading on. It tells Morgan that the truck driver cannot see Morgan. If you cannot see the driver in the side mirror, the driver cannot see you. Lingering in a truck's no-zone makes it harder for the trucker to steer clear of danger, so Morgan should not stay there. And truck drivers cannot see everything around them, even though they sit about twice as high.

lines.text: Slow to speed up; more room to turn and stop.
Drivers sit high but cannot see everything.
Front twenty feet; rear two hundred feet.

narration.text: Let us recap. Heavy trucks gain speed slowly, especially uphill, and their size can make them seem slower than they are. A truck's rear wheels do not follow its front wheels, so it needs extra room to turn; check its turn signal before passing a truck that seems to start a left turn. Truck brakes heat up downhill, so the truck needs more distance to stop, and its wind can affect your steering. Truck drivers sit high but cannot see everything. The no-zones reach up to twenty feet in front, along both sides and up to two hundred feet behind.

why_how.text: The handbook says recreational vehicles are larger and slower than cars and block more of your view.
Vehicles towing trailers can sway or jackknife and take a long stretch of road to pass.

scenario.text: Casey is behind a car towing a trailer on a two-lane road and wants to pass.

reasoning.text: Passing a trailer and its towing vehicle safely can take a half mile of clear road, and braking hard near it risks a jackknife.

result.text: Casey waits for a long stretch of clear road before passing.

claim.text: Common mistake: braking suddenly right in front of a vehicle towing a trailer.

correction.text: Sudden braking can make the trailer jackknife.

prompt.text: Casey wants to pass a car towing a trailer. How much clear road can that take?

rationale.text: Passing a vehicle towing a trailer may need a half mile of clear road.

narration.text: This lesson covers recreational vehicles and vehicles towing trailers. You will review how recreational vehicles compare with cars in size and handling, what happens to your view as you get closer to one, what to watch for near a vehicle towing a trailer, what sudden braking can cause, and how much clear road it can take to pass a trailer and its towing vehicle. The theme is the same as with trucks: these vehicles are larger, slower to respond and harder to see around, so they need more room, and you need more room when passing them.

lines.text: Longer, higher and wider than cars.
Slower to speed up and stop.

narration.text: Recreational vehicles are typically longer, higher and wider than cars, speed up and stop more slowly, and need more turning room. The closer you get to a recreational vehicle, the more it blocks your view, and its driver has much larger blind spots than a car driver. So a recreational vehicle behaves more like a truck than a car. It needs more room to turn, it speeds up and stops more slowly, and following it closely blocks more of what you can see ahead. Its driver also has much larger blind spots than a car driver, so do not assume you are seen.

lines.text: Watch for sway in crosswinds and on curves.
Sudden braking can cause a jackknife.
Passing can take a half mile.

narration.text: Near a vehicle towing a trailer, watch for sway in crosswinds or on slippery curves, and know that sudden braking can make the trailer jackknife. Passing a trailer and its towing vehicle safely can take a half mile of clear road. So a trailer adds two risks and one need. The risks are sway, in crosswinds or on slippery curves, and a jackknife if there is sudden braking. The need is space: passing a trailer and its towing vehicle can take a half mile of clear road, so plan for a long, clear stretch before you start to pass.

lines.text: Passing may need a half mile.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Passing a vehicle towing a trailer may need a half mile of clear road, and braking hard near it risks a jackknife. Practice questions may suggest that a trailer can be passed in a short distance, or that sudden braking near a trailer is harmless. Neither matches the handbook. Plan your pass for a long stretch of clear road, and avoid sudden braking near a vehicle towing a trailer, because sudden braking can make the trailer jackknife. The memory line: long pass, gentle brakes. Both parts come from the same idea, that trailers need room.

Here is a quick check: Casey is behind a car towing a trailer on a two-lane road and wants to pass. How much clear road can it take to pass safely? Work it out before reading on. It can take a half mile of clear road. Passing a trailer and its towing vehicle safely can take a half mile of clear road, and braking hard near it risks a jackknife. So Casey waits for a long, clear stretch before starting the pass. Casey also watches for the trailer to sway in crosswinds or on slippery curves, and avoids braking suddenly near it.

lines.text: RVs: larger, slower, bigger blind spots.
Passing can take a half mile.

narration.text: To finish, recreational vehicles are typically longer, higher and wider than cars, speed up and stop more slowly, and need more turning room. The closer you get, the more one blocks your view, and its driver has much larger blind spots than a car driver. Near a vehicle towing a trailer, watch for sway in crosswinds or on slippery curves, and know that sudden braking can make the trailer jackknife. Passing a trailer and its towing vehicle safely can take a half mile of clear road. Next, motorcycles and mopeds, and how to pass and see them.

why_how.text: The handbook says motorcycle and moped riders get the same right-of-way consideration as any other driver.
Motorcycles and mopeds are passed differently, and both can hide in blind spots.

scenario.text: Taylor comes up behind a moped riding on the right side of the lane and wants to pass.

reasoning.text: Mopeds ride on the right side of the lane, and when passing one you must stay at least two feet to its left.

result.text: Taylor passes with at least two feet of room to the moped's left, leaving enough room that the windstream cannot upset the rider.

claim.text: Common mistake: sharing the lane with a motorcycle while passing it.

correction.text: A motorcycle is entitled to its full lane, so pass it by changing lanes exactly as you would for a larger vehicle.

prompt.text: Taylor is about to pass a moped on the right side of the lane. How much room must Taylor leave?

answer.text: At least two feet to its left.

rationale.text: A motorcycle, by contrast, is passed by changing lanes, because it owns its full lane.

narration.text: This lesson covers how to pass and see motorcycle and moped riders. You will review the right-of-way consideration riders get, how to pass a motorcycle, where mopeds ride and how much room to leave when passing one, why you leave room when passing any cyclist, when to look especially carefully for riders, and what the handbook says about who is usually at fault in North Carolina crashes between cars and motorcycles. Practice questions often test the difference between passing a motorcycle and passing a moped, so that contrast gets its own slide in this lesson.

Give motorcycle and moped riders the same right-of-way consideration as any other driver. So a rider on two wheels is owed the same right-of-way consideration as a driver in a car. The later points in this lesson build on this one. Riders get the same consideration as any other driver, and motorcycles and mopeds can be completely hidden in blind spots, so you also need to look for them. The rest of the lesson covers how to pass them and when to look for them, and what tends to go wrong when car drivers do not. Give motorcycle and moped riders the same right-of-way consideration as any other driver.

lines.text: Change lanes, as for a larger vehicle.

narration.text: A motorcycle is entitled to its full lane, so pass it by changing lanes exactly as you would for a larger vehicle. So when you pass a motorcycle, you do not squeeze by within its lane. You move fully into the other lane, the same way you would pass a car or a truck. The motorcycle's lane belongs to it, the whole width of it. Treat the pass exactly as you would for a larger vehicle: check that the other lane is clear, change lanes, pass, and return to your lane when it is safe. Never share the motorcycle's lane while passing it.

lines.text: Mopeds ride on the right of the lane.
Stay at least two feet to its left.

narration.text: Mopeds ride on the right side of the lane, and when passing one you must stay at least two feet to its left. Leave enough room when passing any cyclist so your vehicle's windstream cannot make the rider lose control. So passing a moped is different from passing a motorcycle. The moped rides on the right side of the lane, and you must keep at least two feet to its left as you pass. And with any cyclist, leave enough room that the windstream from your vehicle cannot make the rider lose control. At least two feet is the minimum.

lines.text: Moped: at least two feet to its left.

narration.text: Here is the trap. To pass a motorcycle you change lanes because it owns its full lane, while to pass a moped you keep at least two feet to its left. Practice questions may apply the two-foot rule to a motorcycle, or require a full lane change for a moped. Both mix up the handbook. A motorcycle is entitled to its full lane, so the pass is a full lane change. A moped rides on the right side of the lane, so you pass it staying at least two feet to its left. The memory line: motorcycle lane, moped gap. Pass the motorcycle with a lane change, and the moped with a gap.

lines.text: Riders can hide completely in blind spots.
Look before turning, changing lanes, pulling out.

narration.text: Motorcycles and mopeds can be completely hidden in blind spots, so look for them before turning, changing lanes or pulling out, especially when turning left. About two-thirds of North Carolina motorcycle crashes involve a car, and in most of them the car driver is at fault, often saying the motorcycle went unseen. So car drivers need to look for riders. Before turning, changing lanes or pulling out, and especially before turning left, look specifically for motorcycles and mopeds, because they can be completely hidden in blind spots.

lines.text: A moped on the right of the lane.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Taylor comes up behind a moped riding on the right side of the lane and is about to pass it. How much room must Taylor leave? Work it out before reading on. Taylor must stay at least two feet to the moped's left. Mopeds ride on the right side of the lane, and when passing one you must stay at least two feet to its left. Taylor should also leave enough room that the windstream cannot make the rider lose control. If it were a motorcycle, Taylor would change lanes, because a motorcycle owns its full lane.

lines.text: Motorcycle: change lanes; moped: two feet.
Look for riders, especially turning left.

narration.text: To wrap up, give motorcycle and moped riders the same right-of-way consideration as any other driver. A motorcycle is entitled to its full lane, so pass it by changing lanes. Mopeds ride on the right side of the lane, and when passing one you must stay at least two feet to its left, leaving enough room that your windstream cannot upset the rider. Riders can be completely hidden in blind spots, so look for them before turning, changing lanes or pulling out, especially turning left. In most car and motorcycle crashes, the car driver is at fault.

why_how.text: The handbook says motorcycles usually stop faster than cars, but not always.
Surface hazards and rough roads can upset riders, so give them room and never crowd them.

scenario.text: Jesse is following a motorcycle carrying a passenger on a road with wet leaves.

reasoning.text: Motorcycles stop more slowly with a passenger or on poor surfaces, and wet leaves can make a rider lose control.

result.text: Jesse leaves a longer following distance and never crowds the motorcycle.

claim.text: Many people think a motorcycle always stops faster than a car.

correction.text: Motorcycles usually stop faster than cars, but more slowly with a passenger or on poor road surfaces.

prompt.text: Jesse is following a motorcycle that carries a passenger. Will it stop faster than a car?

answer.text: Not necessarily; with a passenger it stops more slowly.

rationale.text: Motorcycles usually stop faster than cars, but more slowly with a passenger or on poor surfaces.

narration.text: This lesson covers how much room to give motorcycle and moped riders. You will review how motorcycle stopping compares with car stopping and when motorcycles stop more slowly, which pavement hazards can make a rider ahead lose control, what a wobbling or hesitant rider suggests, why you should never crowd a rider and when to leave a longer following distance, and where riders need extra room. The common thread is that two wheels are easily destabilized, so surface conditions and following distance matter for the rider ahead of you.

Most motorcycles stop faster than cars, but they stop more slowly with a passenger or on poor surfaces where hard braking could cause a fall. So the usual rule has two exceptions. A motorcycle carrying a passenger stops more slowly, and so does a motorcycle on a poor surface, where hard braking could cause a fall. When you follow a motorcycle, notice whether it carries a passenger and what the road surface is like. Either one can mean the motorcycle stops more slowly than you might expect, so leave room for it. A passenger or a poor surface means a slower stop.

lines.text: Slower with a passenger or on poor surfaces.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Motorcycles usually stop faster than cars, but more slowly with a passenger or on poor road surfaces. Practice questions may say a motorcycle always stops faster than a car, or always stops more slowly. Neither matches the handbook. The usual case is faster, but a passenger or a poor road surface makes it stop more slowly. When a question mentions a passenger, or sand, gravel or wet pavement, expect the slower stop. When it describes a solo rider on a good surface, expect the usual faster stop. Read the conditions before you answer.

lines.text: Extra room on rails, rough roads, metal.

narration.text: Sand, gravel, wet leaves or water on the pavement can make a rider ahead lose control, and a wobbling or hesitant rider is likely a beginner who needs extra room. Never crowd a motorcycle or moped, and leave a longer following distance on slippery roads because two wheels are easily destabilized. Give riders extra room at railroad crossings, on rough roads and on metal surfaces such as steel bridge joints and grating. So watch the surface ahead of the rider, watch how the rider handles, and give extra room whenever the road could upset two wheels.

Here is a quick check: Jesse is following a motorcycle that is carrying a passenger, on a road covered with wet leaves. Will the motorcycle stop faster than a car? Work it out before reading on. Not necessarily. Most motorcycles stop faster than cars, but they stop more slowly with a passenger or on poor surfaces. Wet leaves on the pavement can also make a rider lose control. So Jesse should never crowd the motorcycle, and should leave a longer following distance, because on slippery roads two wheels are easily destabilized.

lines.text: Usually faster stops, but not loaded or on poor surfaces.
Never crowd; longer gap when slippery.
Extra room at rails, rough roads, metal.

narration.text: Let us recap. Most motorcycles stop faster than cars, but more slowly with a passenger or on poor surfaces where hard braking could cause a fall. Sand, gravel, wet leaves or water can make a rider ahead lose control, and a wobbling or hesitant rider is likely a beginner who needs extra room. Never crowd a motorcycle or moped, and leave a longer following distance on slippery roads. Give riders extra room at railroad crossings, on rough roads and on metal surfaces such as steel bridge joints and grating. Next, the rules that apply to mopeds themselves.

why_how.text: The handbook defines a moped by its motor and top speed and sets an operator age.
Mopeds must be registered and plated, and riders must wear helmets and ride visibly.

scenario.text: Dana, who is sixteen with a valid N.C. driver license, is buying a moped whose motor is no more than fifty cubic centimeters with no external shifting device.

reasoning.text: A moped's top speed may not exceed thirty miles per hour, and every moped must be registered with the DMV and display a rear license plate.

result.text: Dana registers the moped, mounts the plate on the rear and wears a helmet with the strap fastened.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a moped needs no registration or plate.

correction.text: Every moped must be registered with the DMV and display a license plate on the rear at all times.

prompt.text: Dana wants to ride a moped on a public road. What is the minimum age, and what card is needed?

answer.text: At least sixteen, with a valid N.C. driver license or ID card.

rationale.text: A moped is limited to a motor of fifty cubic centimeters and a top speed of thirty miles per hour, and its operator must be at least sixteen.

narration.text: This lesson covers the rules for mopeds themselves. You will review how North Carolina defines a moped, its top speed limit, who may operate one on a public road, the helmet rule for riders and passengers, how moped riders should position themselves and make themselves visible, the registration and license plate rule, and what an owner can use as proof of ownership without the certificate of origin. Practice questions often test the three moped limits together, the motor size, the top speed and the operator age, so those get their own slide in this lesson.

lines.text: Motor no more than fifty cubic centimeters.
Top speed no more than thirty mph.

narration.text: North Carolina defines a moped as a two- or three-wheeled vehicle with a motor of no more than fifty cubic centimeters and no external shifting device. A moped's top speed may not exceed thirty miles per hour, and mopeds built to go faster are illegal to use in North Carolina. So the definition has three parts: two or three wheels, a motor of no more than fifty cubic centimeters, and no external shifting device. On top of that, the top speed may not exceed thirty miles per hour, and a moped built to go faster is illegal to use in North Carolina.

lines.text: Valid N.C. driver license or ID card.

narration.text: To operate a moped on a public road you must be at least sixteen and hold a valid N.C. driver license or ID card, and impaired driving laws apply to moped riders too. Moped riders and all passengers must wear a helmet meeting the federal motor vehicle safety standard, with the retention strap fastened. So a moped operator needs both the minimum age and a valid license or ID card, and the impaired driving laws apply just as they do to drivers. The helmet rule covers every moped rider and every passenger, regardless of age, with the strap fastened.

Here is the trap. A moped is limited to a motor of fifty cubic centimeters and a top speed of thirty miles per hour, and its operator must be at least sixteen. Practice questions may swap these numbers, offering a thirty cubic centimeter motor or a fifty mile per hour top speed, or a different age. Keep each number with its limit. Fifty belongs to the motor, in cubic centimeters. Thirty belongs to the top speed, in miles per hour. Sixteen belongs to the operator's minimum age. The memory line: motor, speed, age limits, in that order: fifty, thirty, sixteen.

lines.text: Keep right; never share a lane.
Never squeeze between parked cars and traffic.

narration.text: Moped riders should keep right in the lane, never share a lane with another vehicle, and never squeeze between parked cars and moving traffic at an intersection. Moped riders should wear light or bright clothing and use electric turn signals if fitted, or hand signals otherwise. So a moped rider stays on the right side of the lane but keeps the lane to itself, without sharing it with another vehicle. At intersections, the rider does not squeeze between parked cars and moving traffic. And the rider makes themselves easy to see with bright clothing and clear signals.

lines.text: Registered with the DMV since July two thousand fifteen.
Rear license plate at all times.
Affidavit of facts as ownership proof.

narration.text: Since July of two thousand fifteen, every moped must be registered with the DMV and display a license plate on the rear at all times. A moped owner without the manufacturer's certificate of origin can use an affidavit of facts form as proof of ownership. So every moped needs DMV registration and a rear plate that is always displayed. If the owner does not have the manufacturer's certificate of origin, the affidavit of facts form can serve as proof of ownership instead, so the moped can still be registered. Registration and a rear plate are required for every moped.

lines.text: Dana wants to ride on a public road.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Dana wants to ride a moped on a public road. What is the minimum age, and what card must Dana hold? Work it out before reading on. Dana must be at least sixteen and hold a valid N.C. driver license or ID card. Impaired driving laws apply to moped riders too. A moped is limited to a motor of fifty cubic centimeters and a top speed of thirty miles per hour, and its operator must be at least sixteen. Dana and any passenger must also wear a helmet with the retention strap fastened. The helmet rule covers riders and passengers alike.

lines.text: Fifty cubic centimeters, thirty mph, age sixteen.

narration.text: To finish, North Carolina defines a moped as a two- or three-wheeled vehicle with a motor of no more than fifty cubic centimeters and no external shifting device, and its top speed may not exceed thirty miles per hour. To operate one on a public road you must be at least sixteen with a valid N.C. driver license or ID card. Riders and all passengers must wear a helmet with the strap fastened. Keep right, never share a lane, and wear bright clothing. Every moped must be registered with the DMV and display a rear plate, and an affidavit of facts can prove ownership.

why_how.text: The handbook says littering is illegal in North Carolina, and the driver is held responsible for litter from the vehicle.
A repeat littering conviction carries a higher fine than a first.

scenario.text: A passenger in Lee's car tosses a wrapper out the window.

reasoning.text: The driver is held responsible when litter is thrown or blown from the vehicle.

result.text: Lee, as the driver, is held responsible for the litter.

claim.text: Many people think only the person who threw the litter is responsible.

correction.text: Littering is illegal in North Carolina, and the driver is held responsible when litter is thrown or blown from the vehicle.

prompt.text: Trash blows out of the open bed of Lee's pickup. Who is held responsible?

rationale.text: The driver is held responsible whether litter is thrown or blown from the vehicle.

narration.text: This last lesson in the chapter covers littering. You will review that littering is illegal in North Carolina, who is held responsible when litter comes from a vehicle, and how the fine for a repeat littering offense compares with the fine for a first conviction. This is a short lesson with only two rules, but practice questions like to test who is responsible, because many people assume the person who threw the litter is the only one held responsible. The handbook places the responsibility on the driver, whether the litter is thrown or blown from the vehicle.

lines.text: Thrown or blown from the vehicle.

narration.text: Littering is illegal in North Carolina, and the driver is held responsible when litter is thrown or blown from the vehicle. So the rule covers two ways litter can leave a vehicle. It may be thrown from the vehicle, or it may be blown from the vehicle. In both cases, the driver is the one held responsible. It does not matter who threw it, or whether anyone threw it at all. Littering is illegal in North Carolina in either case, and the responsibility for litter that leaves the vehicle rests with the driver. The driver is held responsible when litter is thrown or blown from the vehicle.

lines.text: Thrown by a passenger: driver responsible.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Many people think only the person who threw the litter is responsible. The handbook says littering is illegal in North Carolina, and the driver is held responsible when litter is thrown or blown from the vehicle. Practice questions may offer the passenger, or no one at all, as the responsible person when a passenger throws litter or when it blows out by accident. Neither matches the handbook. Whether the litter was thrown or blown, and whoever threw it, the driver is held responsible. The memory line: driver owns the litter.

lines.text: First conviction: two hundred fifty to one thousand dollars.
Repeat within three years: five hundred to two thousand.

narration.text: A first littering conviction is fined two hundred fifty dollars to one thousand dollars, while a repeat within three years is fined five hundred dollars to two thousand dollars. So the fine for a repeat offense within three years is higher, at both ends of the range, than the fine for a first conviction. The low end rises from two hundred fifty dollars to five hundred dollars, and the high end rises from one thousand dollars to two thousand dollars. Fine amounts are set by law and can change, so the current figures should be checked with the state before relying on them.

lines.text: Trash blows out of a pickup bed.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Lee is driving a pickup truck, and loose trash blows out of the open bed onto the road. Nobody threw it. Who is held responsible? Work it out before reading on. Lee, the driver, is held responsible. Littering is illegal in North Carolina, and the driver is held responsible when litter is thrown or blown from the vehicle. It does not matter that nobody threw it. If Lee were convicted a second time within three years, the fine would be higher than for a first conviction, as the previous slide described.

To finish the chapter, littering is illegal in North Carolina, and the driver is held responsible when litter is thrown or blown from the vehicle. A first littering conviction is fined two hundred fifty dollars to one thousand dollars, while a repeat within three years is fined five hundred dollars to two thousand dollars. This chapter has covered sharing the road with bicyclists, pedestrians, trucks, recreational vehicles, trailers, motorcycles and mopeds, and the moped rules themselves. Each of them has its own rules for passing, room and visibility.
